opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's funny — I was really lucky with the timing. I started my PhD at Stanford with Fei-Fei right around 2012, 2013, so AlexNet had just happened and the whole field was in this moment of realizing that deep learning on ImageNet actually works. Everything was changing under our feet.

One big lesson I took from that era was about the power of scaling data and compute together with fairly simple, general methods. ImageNet wasn't just a benchmark. It was a bet that if you collect data at a scale nobody thought was reasonable, the algorithms will eventually catch up and do something remarkable with it. That bet paid off in a big way, and it shaped how I think about what comes next.

The other thing I noticed, especially toward the end of my PhD, was how limited image classification is as a task. Putting a label on a picture is useful, but it isn't really understanding the visual world. That's why a lot of my work moved toward richer outputs: dense captioning, scene graphs, connecting vision and language, and then generative work like style transfer and image generation from structured inputs. I kept trying to push past "what's in this image" toward something more like "what's going on here, and how does it all fit together."

More and more, I've come to believe the next frontier is three-dimensional and spatial. Our world isn't a collection of 2D pictures. It's a 3D world that unfolds in time, and we move through it and act on it. A lot of what ImageNet-era vision did was treat images as flat arrays of pixels, which got us very far. But if you want systems that can really perceive, reason about, and interact with the world, they need some kind of spatial understanding. They need to model geometry, physics, and how things change when you move or act.

So in some ways I see the same pattern repeating. Back then the question was how to get the data and the models to scale for 2D recognition. Now the question is how to do that for 3D, for world models, for spatial intelligence. The ingredients are different: different data, different representations, and very different compute demands. But that early lesson still holds. Find the right general formulation, scale it up, and be patient enough to let it surprise you.

r001.rationale: The response says computer vision should advance toward 3D spatial intelligence that can perceive, reason about, and interact with the world, but it does not state that AI should move from data centers into the physical world.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I started my PhD at Stanford in 2012, which is basically the exact moment AlexNet came out, and that timing really shaped everything. I got to live through the period where every few months some long-standing benchmark would just fall. ImageNet classification, then detection, then segmentation, captioning, visual question answering. There was this incredible sense that if you could write down a dataset and a loss function, a neural network would eventually just solve it.

But the thing I came away with, maybe more than the excitement, was a sense of how much ImageNet had quietly defined the field. It wasn't just a benchmark, it was a worldview. It said vision is about taking a single 2D image and producing a label, or a box, or a mask. And an enormous amount of the progress of that era was really about getting better and better at that particular framing. The architectures, the training recipes, the pretraining and fine-tuning paradigm, all of it was downstream of "image goes in, discrete semantic thing comes out."

And at some point I started to feel like that framing was running out. Not because the models were bad, but because the problems were getting saturated and the interesting questions weren't about labels anymore. Images are projections of a 3D world. Objects have shape, they occupy space, there's lighting and materials and motion over time. A system that can tell you "dog" with ninety-nine percent accuracy still has basically no idea what a dog is as a physical thing. So that's what pushed me toward 3D, toward differentiable rendering, toward things like generating meshes from single images and eventually neural scene representations. I wanted vision to be about recovering the structure of the world rather than just naming things in a picture.

The other lesson from that era, which I think is still true, is that the field moves when the data and the tooling move. ImageNet unlocked a decade of progress because it existed at the right scale and the right time. Caffe and then PyTorch unlocked a lot because they let people iterate fast. So when I think about what comes next, I think less about any specific architecture and more about what the ImageNet moment looks like for 3D and for video, where the raw data is everywhere but the supervision is much harder to get. And honestly, a lot of the answer is turning out to be that the supervision is learned rather than labeled, which is a pretty different world from the one I started in.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward 3D, video, and recovering the structure of the world, but it does not state that the next decade will focus on moving AI out of data centers and into the physical world.

astra-6.text:
The ImageNet era was really formative for me because it showed how quickly a field could change when you had the right combination of data, compute, and a method that actually worked. You could learn representations from pixels that were much more powerful than the features we’d been designing by hand.

But it also made the limitations of the task more apparent. You take an image, and the system gives you one label. That’s an incredibly useful benchmark, but there’s a huge gap between recognizing that there’s a dog in a picture and understanding what’s happening in that scene—how objects relate to each other, what might happen next, or what the scene looks like from another viewpoint.

So the question for me became: how do we move beyond assigning labels toward richer models of the visual world? Generation is a particularly interesting way to push on that. If you ask a model to construct an image, it has to capture details that a classifier might be able to ignore. That doesn’t automatically mean it understands everything, but it gives us a different way to explore what these representations have actually learned.

r001.rationale: The response says the ImageNet era prompted interest in richer visual-world models and generation, but it does not say the next decade should move AI from data centers into the physical world.

sol-6.1.text:
The ImageNet era was really formative for me. You had this concrete task, a dataset, and a number everyone was trying to improve. And once deep learning started working, you could see progress happening incredibly quickly. That was exciting because it suggested we could learn representations instead of designing every piece of a vision system by hand.

But it also made me think about what the task was leaving out. Recognizing that an image contains a chair is useful, but it doesn’t tell you how that chair occupies space, what it looks like from another viewpoint, or how you could interact with it. Getting better at classification wasn’t necessarily going to give us all of those things automatically.

So the question for me became: how do we move from recognizing images to understanding the visual world? That pulls you toward connecting vision with language, toward generation, and toward 3D. Can a system describe relationships between objects? Can it construct a scene? Can it predict what changes when you move the camera? ImageNet showed how powerful learning could be. The next step was figuring out what we should ask these systems to learn.

r001.rationale: The response says the next step was understanding the visual world through language, generation, and 3D, but does not say computer vision should move AI from data centers into the physical world.
